title: Hierarchical Goal Abstractions via Learned Subset Relations
claim: Goals form a partially ordered hierarchy, and following directed edges turns a concrete goal into increasingly abstract ones.
layout: 1 wide panel, left-to-right columns, directed arrows converging, concrete-to-abstract labels
description: A wide figure split into vertical blue columns. The left column is labeled 'Most concrete, g⊥' and holds a single maze/map image. The right column is labeled 'Most abstract, g⊤' and holds the same map with every free-space region filled in bright yellow. Between them, grey maze thumbnails carry heat-map blobs that show goal distributions. Three rows branch out from the concrete goal. Each starts as a small bright dot in one room. Moving right, the blobs grow and merge, so two or more rooms are highlighted together. White triangular arrows show the directed partial-order edges. They branch out from the first image and converge in later columns. An ellipsis sits before the final abstract goal. The eye goes first to the bright yellow final image and the dot-to-region progression.
caption: Traversing the latent goal space. Directed edges denote the partial order, showing that abstract goals can be formed by either
abstract: In self-supervised goal-conditioned reinforcement learning (RL) without external rewards, goals are typically specified by observations sampled from experience. However, depending on the observation structure, such a fixed representation of goals may be either too concrete (requiring exact pixel-level matches) or too abstract (involving ambiguous observations). Here we propose the construction of hierarchical latent goal spaces that integrate both concrete and abstract goals. To this end, we use an energy function to learn a partially ordered space, in which a subset relation between observations naturally induces a hierarchy from concrete to abstract goals. This representation enables agents to disambiguate specific states while also generalizing to shared concepts. In experiments on navigation and robotic manipulation, agents trained with our hierarchical goal space achieve higher task success and greater generalization to novel tasks compared to agents limited to purely observational goals.
